catalog_quote: Une phrase interrogative semble avoir surtout deux intona- tions, d'après que la phrase ordinaire a des tons hauts ou non . S'il y a des tons hauts, les intervalles sont plus grands : ( - nurukoba rwaanjye ? est - ce ma peau ? -), et les tons préparatoires sont plus marqués, au détriment du ton haut même : agatsíma karasígaye, il reste un peu de pâte ... S'il y avait un accent d'intensité caractérisant l'un ou l'autre élément, on s'attendrait à une prononciation différente de paires de mots comme la suivante : ba - ra - ru - tan - a ils l'étirent ( la peau) ba - ra - rut - an - a ils se surpassent l'un l'autre Or on dit indifféremment dans les deux cas : bararutana . MORPHOLOGIE La morphologie comprendra, après une introduction morphonologique, [running header:] 20 ESSAI DE GRAMMAIRE RUNDI.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Rundi (rund1242) is not in the catalog. The two title-hit items could not be read: Philippson's 1991/92 Paris 5 thèse d'État 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale' (542 pp., Rundi among 47 languages) exists only in print/ANRT reproduction (theses.fr 'accessible: non'; not on HAL, archive.org, DDL or LLACAN pages) — its abstract frames East Bantu prosody as a scale from fully tonal to penultimate demarcative stress, but says nothing Rundi-specific; priority high as the best comparative accent source. Its published summary (Philippson 1998, Faits de langues 11-12: 429-440, Persée) was found but the PDF is bot-blocked (not reachable by automated download). Rodegem 1962 'Vocabulaire accentué' (ronéotypé, 90 pp.) is a tone-marked wordlist with no trace anywhere online (SUDOC 0, archive.org 0; priority low. Best first-hand statement read: Stevick 1965 FSI Kirundi Basic Course pp. 12-15 — two tones LOW/HIGH, mora-based placement, no stress anywhere in the book; Ménard 1908 §§53-62/474-482 gives placement rules for a lexical 'accent' that is high tone/length, and Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 p. 40 report one High per phonological word in non-focus verbs ('more like an accentual language'). No source read states a word-stress rule for Rundi; it should be recorded as a tone language (no stress record), with Meeussen 1959 / Rodegem 1967 / Philippson 1991 as the print sources still to be checked. all look-ups were direct downloads and catalog APIs. new_statements.quote: In Kirundi however, as in most African languages, pitch has functions which it does not have in English. [...] Pitch, then, may be the only audible difference between two words of entirely different meanings. To say the same thing in technical terms, Kirundi has LEXICALLY SIGNIFICANT distinctions of pitch. [p. 11] [...] In Kirundi, as in many other Bantu languages, the pitch phenomena are best described in terms of two tones, called LOW [and] HIGH. Low tone is quite simple: its typical realization is as a level, relatively low pitch [...] As its name implies, high tone ordinarily involves the use of a relatively high pitch, but this pitch is not level. [p. 13]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kirundi is described as a two-tone (High/Low) language in which pitch is lexically and grammatically distinctive and is counted on moras (short vowel = 1 mora, long = 2); the source describes tone placement per verb form and noun class and never invokes stress or intensity prominence. No source opened states a word-stress position, and none explicitly denies stress. Later analyses (Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989: 40; Jouannet 1989: 11-12) call the system 'accentual' in the pitch accent sense (at most one High per phonological word in non-focus verb forms), not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tone: 'anticipated' high tone spills onto the preceding syllable; a 'provisional high tone' on /ni/, /si/ appears only after a non-pause (Stevick 1965: 21). Ménard 1908 (pp. 19-25, 282-286) gives lexical placement rules for his 'accent', which is high tone/length, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone described on citation forms and in sentence frames (FSI dialogues); Stevick notes utterance-final vs non-final differences in tone realization (e.g. twaakubuuye forms, p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe standard Kirundi of Burundi (rund1242; ISO run). The FSI course was prepared with Barundi speakers who lack the j/jy, c/cy, sh/shy contrasts 'present in some dialects' (Stevick 1965: xlvi); Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 use Sabimana's own judgments. Ménard 1908 is the same language a century earlier (missionary orthography).

new_statements.quote: In Kirundi, as in many other Bantu languages, the pitch phenomena are best described in terms of two tones, called LOW [and] HIGH. Low tone is quite simple: its typical realization is as a level, relatively low pitch [...] As its name implies, high tone ordinarily involves the use of a relatively high pitch, but this pitch is not level. It most commonly consists of a rise followed immediately by a fall [...] A MORA is a unit of vowel length. Vowels in Kirundi may consist of either one or two moras, and no more. [...] The high tone may be attached to a vowel (whether long or short) at either of two PITCH POINTS. [...] There is never more than one high tone per mora
new_statements.citation: Stevick, Earl W. (with Raymond Setukura et al.) 1965. Kirundi Basic Course. Washington DC: Foreign Service Institute, US Department of State. catalog record, Note 1 'The use of the terms pitch and tone', pp. 12-15.
new_statements.locator: catalog record, Note 1, pp. 12-13 (scan pp. 12-13 of the 589-page PDF)
new_statements.reading: Kirundi word prosody is a two-tone (H/L) system with mora-sensitive placement of H; the book (589 pp.) never mentions stress. This is the clearest first-hand, English-language description read in this search of works with stress in the title. Two refinements read alongside it: Ménard 1908 §§53-62 (pp. 19-24) and §§474-482 (pp. 282-285) give placement rules for a lexically distributed 'accent' (grave mark, 'équivaut à peu près à notre accent circonflexe'; monosyllabic radicals and final syllables never take it, radical-initial vowels and vowels before NC usually do) which is the pre-tonological rendering of high tone/length, not stress; Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 (Modèles en tonologie, p. 40) note that in non-focus verb forms 'there can be only one High tone per phonological word', so these forms 'look more like an accentual language than a tone language', and (p. 20) that tone-shift rules are sensitive to odd/even mora counts, 'found to date only in metrical stress systems'. Net: no source read states a word-stress position for Rundi; it is coded in the literature as a tone language with a culminative (one-H-per-word) accentual tendency in part of the verb system.

sources.note: §3 'De l'accent' §§53-62 pp. 19-25 and Supplément §§474-482 pp. 282-286: 'L'accent tonique ordinaire équivaut à peu près à notre accent circonflexe' (p. 20); place of the 'accent' is lexical and given by lists/rules (monosyllabic roots never take it; final syllables always short; disyllabic roots either unaccented or accented on the first syllable; vowel-initial roots, contracted vowels, vowels before prenasalised C, Cw syllables take it). This 'accent' (grave mark) is the pre-tonological rendering of high tone/length, not stress in the modern sense.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale. (theses.fr abstract) — 'These systems range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), all intermediate cases being represented ... the main driver of the evolution of these systems was the emergence of a demarcative penultimate accent serving as a domain boundary for tone association.'
sources.note: Comparative typology of tone and accent across ~30-47 East Bantu languages (Glottolog lists Rundi [run] among the 47 covered). The abstract places languages on a scale from purely tonal to purely penultimate-stress; where Rundi sits on that scale is not stated in the abstract, and the Rundi section was not read. No open copy exists: not on HAL (16 Philippson records, none the thesis), archive.org, Persée; DDL Lyon staff page lists it without a PDF; theses.fr marks it not accessible. Available only in print / ANRT microfiche. Philippson's 1998 published summary (Faits de langues 11-12: 429-440…
